title: Fibonacci Number
description: Brute force to optimized: recursion, memoization, constant space, and a logarithmic time doubling trick.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a number n, find the n-th Fibonacci number, where each value is the sum of the two before it.

blocks.text: Given a number n, find the n-th Fibonacci number. F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1 are given directly, and every number after that is the sum of the two numbers before it: F(n) = F(n minus 1) + F(n minus 2).

blocks.title: Analogy: The Ladder Built From Its Own Last Two Rungs
blocks.text: Picture climbing a ladder where every new rung is built on the spot by welding together the two rungs just below it. To build rung 5, a builder needs rung 4 and rung 3 already in place. To build rung 4, they needed rung 3 and rung 2. The first two rungs, rung 0 and rung 1, are simply bolted to the ground to start with. This is exactly how each Fibonacci number is built from the two immediately before it, and it is also why building rungs out of order wastes work: rung 3 gets welded fresh every single time someone needs it unless it is kept around.

blocks.caption: How each Fibonacci number is built from the two before it

blocks.text: The smallest possible input. F(0) is a base case defined directly in the problem, equal to 0, with no addition needed at all.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what the recurrence itself is really asking for.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The recurrence F(n) = F(n minus 1) + F(n minus 2) means computing F(n) directly asks for two smaller versions of the exact same problem.

Observation 2: Those two smaller calls are not independent, F(n minus 1)'s own recursion also needs F(n minus 2), so the same subproblem gets asked for from multiple places.

Observation 3: If a subproblem's answer never changes once computed, computing it more than once is pure waste, remembering it the first time removes all the repeated work.

Observation 4: Once repeated work is removed, only the most recent couple of values are ever actually needed to move forward, everything older can be forgotten.
That reasoning alone already sketches the whole optimization path: cache the repeated work first, then notice the cache itself can shrink down to just two numbers.
The most direct translation of the definition is plain recursion: F(n) calls itself for F(n minus 1) and F(n minus 2), which each call themselves again, all the way down to the base cases.

items: If n is 0 or 1, return n directly, these are the base cases.
Otherwise, recursively compute F(n minus 1).
Recursively compute F(n minus 2).
Return the sum of those two results.

blocks.caption: Recursion tree for F(4). Notice F(2) and F(1) each get rebuilt more than once

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The base case check, n <= 1, has to come before the recursive calls, otherwise fib(0) or fib(1) would recurse into indices that were never defined.

Both recursive calls are made unconditionally in the same return statement, which is exactly what causes the same smaller subproblems to be asked for repeatedly from different branches of the call tree.
Nothing is cached or remembered between calls, this version exists specifically to make the exponential blowup visible before fixing it.

blocks.text: This works because it is a direct, faithful copy of the mathematical definition, every call eventually bottoms out at the base cases F(0) and F(1).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 to the power n). Every call branches into two more calls, and the same smaller values get recomputed from scratch over and over.
Space: O(n), for the depth of the recursive call stack at any one time.

Limitation: the diagram above shows F(2) being fully rebuilt twice just to compute F(4), and the overlap gets dramatically worse as n grows, this is what causes the exponential blow up. The two calls being made are not independent problems, they share huge amounts of repeated work.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the recursion itself is not the problem: the recurrence is correct, every call eventually reaches a base case.

What it wastes: the exact same F(k) gets recomputed from scratch every single time a different branch of the recursion needs it.

Can repeated work be avoided: yes, remembering a subproblem's answer the first time it is computed means every later request for it becomes a free lookup.

What structure remembers it: a cache, a dictionary or hash map, from n to its already computed F(n).

The core idea: check the cache before recursing, and store every newly computed result immediately after computing it.

The recursion itself is not the problem, the repeated recomputation of the exact same subproblem is. Once F(2) has been computed a single time, every later call that needs F(2) again should simply reuse that answer instead of rebuilding it.
The optimization is to remember every result the first time it is computed, in a cache, and check that cache before doing any recursive work.

Keep a cache (a dictionary or hash map) from n to its already computed F(n). Before recursing, check the cache. Only do the actual addition when a value has never been seen before, and store the result immediately afterward.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: check the cache before ever recomputing anything

blocks.text: This works because a memoized call and a non-memoized call compute the mathematically identical value, the cache only changes how many times that value gets computed, never what it computes. Every subproblem still gets solved correctly by the same recurrence, it just gets solved once instead of potentially many times.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["n is 0 or 1","Returned immediately as a base case, never touches the cache","F(0) = 0 or F(1) = 1"],["n has been computed before","Found directly in the cache","The previously computed value, no recursion re-run"],["n has not been computed before","Computed via the recurrence, then stored in the cache before returning","A freshly computed value every future call can reuse"]]}

items: The cache is checked before doing any recursive work, so a value that has already been solved short circuits immediately instead of re-entering the recursion.
The result is stored in the cache right before it is returned, guaranteeing every value is written to the cache exactly once, the very first time it is computed.
The cache is passed down through every recursive call so that all branches of the recursion see the same shared cache, not separate copies.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n). Each value from 0 to n is computed exactly once.
Space: O(n), for the cache holding every computed value plus the recursive call stack.

The cache stores every single F(0) through F(n), but computing F(n) only ever actually needs the two most recent values at any point. Everything older than that is kept around but never looked at again.

Intuition: instead of a growing cache, keep just two variables representing the previous two Fibonacci numbers, and slide them forward one step at a time in a simple loop, no recursion and no cache at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","prev","curr","Action","Why"],"rows":[["Start","0","1","F(0), F(1)","These are the two base cases, the starting window before any looping begins."],["1","1","1","next = 0 + 1, shift forward","Combines the current window into the next Fibonacci number, then slides the window one step."],["2","1","2","next = 1 + 1, shift forward","Same sliding step repeated, only the last two values are ever needed."],["3","2","3","next = 1 + 2, shift forward","Same sliding step repeated."],["4","3","5","next = 2 + 3, shift forward","Final slide, curr now holds F(5)."]]}

blocks.caption: Constant space flow: only ever two numbers in memory

items: Only two variables, prev and curr, are ever kept in memory, since computing the next Fibonacci number only ever needs the two immediately before it, matching the recurrence exactly.
Both variables update together in one simultaneous step, so the new curr is computed before prev is overwritten, never accidentally using an already-updated value.
The loop runs from 2 up to n specifically because F(0) and F(1) are already the starting values of prev and curr before the loop even begins.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), still one step per number from 2 up to n.
Space: O(1), just two integers regardless of how large n is, a genuine drop from the O(n) cache used before.

O(n) time means computing F(1000000) takes a million steps. There is a mathematical shortcut that gets this down to O(log n): the doubling identities. Given F(k) and F(k+1), the value at exactly double the index can be computed directly, without walking through every step in between: F(2k) = F(k) times (2 times F(k+1) minus F(k)), and F(2k+1) = F(k) squared plus F(k+1) squared.

Intuition: this is the same idea as fast exponentiation, halve the problem size on every recursive step instead of shrinking it by one. To find F(n), recursively find the pair for n divided by 2, then combine that pair using the two formulas above to jump straight to F(n).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","k","Returns (F(k), F(k+1))","Why"],"rows":[["fibPair(0)","0","(0, 1)","Base case, F(0) and F(1) given directly."],["fibPair(1)","1","(1, 1)","k is odd, built from fibPair(0) using the odd branch formula."],["fibPair(2)","2","(1, 2)","k is even, built from fibPair(1) using the even branch formula."],["fibPair(5)","5","(5, 8)","k is odd, built from fibPair(2) using the odd branch formula, giving F(5) = 5."]]}

blocks.caption: Logarithmic time flow: halve n on every recursive step

items: fibPair returns both F(k) and F(k+1) together, not just F(k) alone, because the doubling identities for F(2k) and F(2k+1) both need access to that consecutive pair, not a single value.
Recursing on k divided by 2 instead of k minus 1 is what turns a linear number of calls into a logarithmic one, the problem size is cut in half on every single call instead of shrinking by one.
The even and odd branch at the end exists because F(2 times half) and F(2 times half plus 1) are two different formulas, and k itself can land on either side of that doubling depending on its value.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), since n is halved on every recursive call, this is a genuine asymptotic improvement over every earlier solution.
Space: O(log n) for the recursive call stack, which matches how many times n can be halved before reaching 0.

blocks.text: This problem is a complete tour of one of the most common progressions in interviews: notice overlapping subproblems, cache them, notice you only need a small sliding window of that cache, then look for a mathematical shortcut that changes the complexity class entirely. Each step is a genuinely different idea, not just a smaller constant.

items: Writing the brute force recursion without ever mentioning or recognizing its exponential blow up.
Forgetting the base cases for both F(0) and F(1), not just F(0).
Stopping at the memoized O(n) solution when interviewers often explicitly ask "can you do better", expecting the constant space or logarithmic time follow up.

blocks.text: Fibonacci is rarely asked for the final answer alone, it is used to see how far a candidate can push an optimization once the obvious solution is on the board. Walking through brute force, then memoization, then constant space, then explicitly asking "should I show the logarithmic approach too" demonstrates real command of the trade-offs rather than a single memorized trick.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the exponential blowup", think: memoize the recursive calls.
If the interviewer says "can you do this with less memory", think: only the last two values are ever needed, drop the cache for two variables.
If the interviewer says "can you do better than O(n)", think: the fast doubling identities bring this down to O(log n).

items: Can you go from the exponential brute force straight to O(1) space, explaining every step in between?
What is the fast doubling identity, and why does halving k on every call produce a logarithmic number of calls?
How would you handle an n large enough that the answer overflows a normal integer type?
Can you compute F(n) iteratively using matrix exponentiation instead of the doubling identities?
What changes if you needed every value from F(0) to F(n), not just F(n) alone?
Any recurrence relation problem where a value depends on a small, fixed number of previous values; climbing stairs and the tribonacci sequence follow the exact same cache-then-shrink progression.
Overlapping subproblems in general, the core signal for reaching for memoization or bottom up dynamic programming in any problem.
Fast exponentiation and other halve-the-problem-size tricks, the fast doubling identity here is structurally the same idea as computing x to the power n in O(log n) multiplications.
Rolling or sliding window state, keeping only the last k values instead of a full history, as a general space optimization once a full cache has already been shown to work.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force is O(2 to the power n) time and O(n) space. Memoization brings time down to O(n) at O(n) space. The constant space version keeps O(n) time but drops space to O(1). The fast doubling version is the strongest of all: O(log n) time and O(log n) space, a genuine change in complexity class, not just a smaller constant.

items: Pattern: overlapping subproblems solved by caching, then shrinking the cache to a sliding window, then replaced entirely by a closed form doubling identity.

Core Idea: F(n) only ever depends on the two values immediately before it, so nothing older ever needs to be kept once those two are known; and the doubling identities let two indices combine directly without walking every step in between.
Time: O(2 to the power n) brute force, O(n) for both memoized and constant space versions, O(log n) for fast doubling.
Space: O(n) for brute force and memoized, O(1) for constant space, O(log n) call stack for fast doubling.
Most Important Observation: this problem is a complete tour of the standard DP optimization ladder, recognize overlap, cache it, shrink the cache, then look for a genuine closed form shortcut.
Interview Difficulty: easy to get a working answer, but interviewers use repeated "can you do better" follow ups to see how far a candidate can push it.
One line memory trick: only the last two matter, and doubling the index beats counting up to it.
